en: The Yoga Upaniṣads, with the commentary of Śrī Upaniṣad-Brahmayogin. Edited by Paṇḍit Ā. Mahādeva Śāstrī, B.A.
First published 1920 by the Adyar Library and Research Centre.
Mahāvākyopaniṣad.
Data-entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark Dyckowski.
* Revision 0 ñune 14, 2007 * CṣX+ Transliteration of the Mahāvākyopaniṣad
"Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ"— thus [ends] the peace invocation.
Now begins the instruction on direct experience,
the supreme Upaniṣad concerning direct experience, which the venerable Brahmā spoke.
We shall explain [it]. (1) This is more secret than the secret; it should not be taught to one who is not a true disciple, but only to one who is sattvic, introverted, and completely purified. (2)

I worship the state of Rāmacandra, the moon who is liberation while yet embodied (*vikalebara-kaivalya*), whose body is the Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*) that is the established doctrine of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*).

Indeed, this Mahāvākya Upaniṣad, which is a division of the Atharvaṇaveda, stands preeminent by first elucidating that which is Brahman alone— established through the awakening to the impossibility of the phenomenal world and its cause apart from one's own Self. A commentary on this [Upaniṣad] is now begun, based on its brief text.

Having observed that there were no persons of the highest qualification, Brahmā spoke to reveal his own experience, beginning with the word "atha" (now). Why? Because it is "aparokṣa" (directly perceived). First, he speaks of the concealment of the Upaniṣad—which is about to be described—due to its secret meaning, with the words "guhyāt" (from the secret). [This is for] the common person who lacks the aforementioned means. Why?

Regarding the phrase "should be instructed," it means that [the teaching] should be imparted to one who possesses the quality of *sattva*, who is oriented toward direct perception, and who is endowed with the means such as a qualified teacher, the sacred texts, and so forth. || 2 ||
The nature and function of knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).
Now, having concluded [the discussion of] knowledge and ignorance as the two eyes for bondage and liberation from *saṃsāra*, [it is said]:
"Knowledge is the light, and ignorance is darkness" (3). For indeed, it is darkness...
The world, consisting of the entire infinite multitude of individual souls, from Brahmā down to the immobile beings, is a manifestation of the body;
it is characterized by the worldly activity of intentional actions as proclaimed by all the Vedas.
Regarding the question "What is this Upaniṣad?", he specifies it with the word "atha" (now).

Now, following the attainment of the aforementioned means, for the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), transmigratory existence consists in the appearance of the reality of something other than oneself; the path of engagement, characterized by the thought "it exists," is bondage; the path of withdrawal, characterized by the thought "it does not exist," is liberation.

Regarding the question of what the causes of the three—bondage, liberation, and their connection—are: the eye of knowledge (*vidyā-cakṣus*), by virtue of turning one away from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), is the cause of liberation; the eye of ignorance (*avidyā-cakṣus*), however, by virtue of impelling one toward the thought that "cyclic existence exists," is the cause of bondage. Both of these consist in the form of cognition (*vedana-rūpa*) [that perceives] "cyclic existence does not exist" and "cyclic existence exists."

Having withdrawn— that is, having negated— knowledge and ignorance by means of the eye of wisdom through the realization that no object whatsoever exists apart from Brahman, and having realized that Brahman, established by such negation,
is non-dual and nothing but its own self, the wise one, at the very moment of perfect knowledge, [becomes Brahman].
The remainder of the sentence is "one becomes liberated while in the disembodied state" (*videhamuktaḥ*). Regarding the question of what the eye of ignorance (*avidyā-cakṣus*) is like, he says:
"ignorance" (*avidyā*). That which does not exist apart from Brahman even throughout the three periods of time is this very ignorance;
by that [ignorance], reality is perceived as if it were real—this is the "world of ignorance" (*avidyā-loka*). That indeed is the "eye," the eighth station of ignorance, and that alone is [the eye].

"It is darkness, because it conceals its own measure. [Sūtra 3] To the question, "What is that darkness which is the concealer? he says: "For darkness... For darkness is the phenomenal world of the body (*śarīra-prapañca*), because it is concealed from one's own knowledge or by time; thus, the body itself is the "concealed" (*āśraya*). That very state of ignorance (*avidyā*) and its effects constitute the locus of concealment.
From Brahmā down to the stationary objects, because this world is projected as nothing other than the non-dual Brahman alone—

and because it is conventionally designated as "the phenomenal world" (prapañca)— it should be understood as having a conventional reality (vyāvahārikatva) and an apparent reality (prātibhāsikatva), since it exists only for the duration of its manifestation or appears [as such]. What more?
Regarding its empirical nature and its illusory appearance, it is said:
as long as one's own ignorance persists, [the world] exists for you as something infinite—like the entire universe and like the infinite-cosmic-egg Brahman-egg;
thus, it is composed of infinite and universal ignorance. However, the world of one's own ignorance is [as vast as] the atmosphere.
One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal; one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrayā* [offering];
"We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal," and so forth—thus does one who possesses worldly activity engage in the practice of all desire-driven rituals proclaimed by the entire Veda. || 4 ||
Through the practice of the knowledge of the Self, there is the manifestation of the Supreme Self;
this Self is not darkness. For knowledge is the sun within the heart, the sphere of light to be grasped, and nothing else. This is that sun.

The *haṃsa* (the swan) is "I am He" (*so'ham*), established through the *ajapā* mantra as *brahman*. Having thus perceived it by means of the inhalation and exhalation in both reverse and direct order, and having attained that for a long time,
when one meditates upon the *brahman* within oneself three times, there arises *saccidānanda* (being-consciousness-bliss).
The Supreme Self manifests. || 6 ||
Regarding the point that one's own Self also transmigrates in this way, he says: "This Self is not darkness.

This very Self, established through the negation of the phenomenal world of non-Self, is not darkness, because it is nothing other than the Supreme Light which is non-different from its own inward light. As long as the Self is thus...
He says that for one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), the practice of knowledge (*vidyābhyāsa*) must be performed: "For knowledge indeed...

Knowledge (*vidyā*) is the function of knowing, higher knowledge, perfect knowledge, and the knowledge of reality, [realizing] that Brahman—which cannot tolerate even the scent of anything other than itself—exists as its own non-dual self alone.

The "internal sun" (*kūṭāntarāditya*) refers to that which culminates in the solar consciousness (*cidāditya*), which illumines both the internal and external within the state of one's own base ignorance (*kutsitāsvavidyāpada*);
thus it is called the "consciousness-sun. That very thing is the orb of the light of pure consciousness (*cinmātra-jyotis-maṇḍala*), the mass of its radiance.
Only the knowledge of reality whose object is the non-distinct Brahman alone is to be accepted,

because it is the cause of the final direct realization and because it culminates in Brahman alone. That alone is to be accepted, and not any other knowledge with distinctions whose object is the lower Brahman.
Because it yields results that are delayed by time, this [path] should not be adopted by those who are most intensely desirous of liberation; such is the meaning. || 5 ||

To the question, "What is the means for attaining the knowledge of reality—which is the cause for realizing the knowledge and wisdom that serve as the means for the manifestation of the Supreme Self attained through such knowledge of reality?"—he says: "This one...
[He who is here in the person and he who is yonder in the sun are one. He who knows this thus...]
In accordance with such scriptural passages as these, this sun, which is within the range of our vision, is Brahman;

for when its own adventitious attributes are removed, it is that very [sun] which is Brahman. This very sun, having entered every body through the gates of the eyes, is occupied with the activity of inhalation and exhalation.

The *haṃsa* (the sun), which is "I" (*so'ham*), is offered through the recitation (*japa*) accomplished effortlessly and spontaneously by means of the exhalation and inhalation (*prāṇāpāna*) in both their reverse and natural orders.
Knowledge and higher realization (*vijñāna*) are thus perfected through this practice of the *ajapā*.

Or rather, having attained that right knowledge which is to be accomplished over a long period of time, this wise man [perceives] within the Brahman— which is the self consisting of the three states (waking, dreaming, and deep sleep)— the division into the manifest and so forth, rooted in his own ignorance, through the distinctions of the non-dual, the one-without-a-second, the world-continuum, and the various conceptualizations such as the Virāṭ, Viśva, and others.

When that which is being meditated upon is realized as nothing but Brahman— non-dual, established through the negation of its effects, names, and forms— then there arises the Supreme Self, which is existence-consciousness-bliss, established by the awakening to the impossibility of birth, suffering, and unreal duality.
It manifests; the meaning is that only its own self remains. || 6 ||
This is not the state of the modification of the knowledge of reality;
it is not like the shoreless ocean drenched and filled by the thousand-rayed sun.
This is not the samādhi of night; this is not the perfection of yoga; this is not the dissolution of the mind. That is oneness with Brahman.
7. He who is of solar luster, beyond darkness, having willed all forms and created their names, abides speaking them.
That which the Sustainer (Dhātṛ) first proclaimed, which the wise Śakra declared in the four quarters—he who knows him thus becomes immortal in this world; there is no other path.
A path exists for traveling. By means of sacrifice, the gods sacrificed with sacrifice;
those were the first ordinances of dharma. They have attained the heights of greatness, where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide.
In this way, the flow of the knowledge of reality— which culminates in nothing other than Brahman as it has come to be—

is suffused and vibrantly manifest by the Supreme Reality, which is non-different from the inwardly luminous Self, the Sun of infinite sheaths exemplified by the thousands [of scriptures] beginning with the *Yuga*.
It is like the ocean that encompasses both its shores.

Because it is filled with and identical to the essence of Brahman alone—like a waveless ocean—and because it is full (*pūrṇa*), it does not dissolve; thus it is "alīla" (without play), for it has the nature of Brahman. Indeed, this state cannot be a meditative absorption (*samādhi*), a perfection of yoga (*yogasiddhi*), or the dissolution of the mind (*manolaya*); rather, it is the unity of the inner self and Brahman. What more [is there to say]?
Therefore, he says "Āditya" [in the verse] to indicate that unity with the inward-facing Brahman (*pratyag-brahmaikya*).

That which is established through the negation of all attributes residing in the unity of the outward and inward consciousness—which depends on the relative distinction between the distant and the near—is situated beyond even the darkness distinct from itself. (p. 305)

The sun of consciousness, shining forth with a radiance that is rare due to the calculation of its rising and setting, remains everywhere full in the form of existence, consciousness, and bliss. Having discerned the names and forms belonging to the sphere of ignorance and its effects— which are distinct from itself— the wise man realizes them to be false.

Having reflected and performed a negation, one remains uttering the thought that nothing exists apart from Brahman; only that [Brahman] alone remains. "He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself; he who thus knows it as seedless (nirbīja) becomes indeed seedless."

Because of the scriptural statement regarding the attainment of the state of Brahman simultaneously with sensation (vedanā). And likewise, the Creator himself previously proclaimed this very meaning: "The wise Śakra, whose fame is renowned for his knowledge of Brahman, [declared] that the four directions—east, south, west, and north—and the intermediate directions are the vital breath (prāṇa), the self of consciousness (prajñātman)."

"Worship Me as life and immortality"—thus [the Lord spoke]. As for the fruit of such knowledge, which He proclaimed: "Free from suffering, stainless, a knower of Brahman, he goes toward Brahman itself"—one who knows that the Supreme Self is thus solely one's own self, without a second, is a knower.

According to the Śruti: "Simultaneously with the cessation of sensation, the Supreme Self becomes immortal here; simultaneously with knowledge, the liberated one attains absolute liberation (kaivalya). This bondage arises from ignorance of the Self, and liberation comes from knowledge of the Self. This alone is the unobstructed path for the sake of reaching liberation.

"Other than the knowledge of Brahman, no other path is known. (9) Thus, even the gods, Indra and the others, performed the sacrifice that is the sacrifice [itself]— the Brahman known as Viṣṇu— by means of the sacrifice of knowledge, realizing that Brahman alone remains as non-dual self-only, and that nothing exists apart from Brahman.

Cultivating the realization "I am Brahman," these great ones are liberated while living; for those deities who are objects of the state of being liberated while living, those were their primary qualities— those primary qualities of one liberated while living being humility and so forth, as well as loving-kindness and so forth.

The principal ones became [the progenitors]. Thus, the gods of such majesty—wherein the ancient Sādhyas, a specific class of deities who are liberated while living, reside—aspire for that celestial realm; having attained that heaven, they shine forth. || 10 ||

The meditation on the light of the syllable *praṇava* is "I am He"; I am the Sun, the supreme light; I am the light of the Sun, the auspicious one (*śiva*); I am the light of the Self, the pure one (*śukra*); I am all light, O carrier of the breaths (*asūvahom*). || 11 ||

(p. 306) Regarding the question of what the gods are doing there, he says—“So 'ham” (I am that)—to show that they abide in the contemplation of the unity of the inner and outer consciousnesses: “That which is the supreme light, I am that sun of consciousness;
that which is the light of the sun, I am that Śiva; I who am Śiva, the light of the sun, I am Śukra.”

The inner self non-different from the Supreme Self is the essence of all light; thus, through mutual exchange, I am the supreme light non-different from the inner light—Om. The fourth state of the fourth [syllable], which is the cause of the unity and distinction between the inner and the supreme, is Brahman.
The meaning is that those who meditate thus—"I am indeed the non-dual Self alone"—are being glorified even today.
This is the fruit of the *Haṃsajyoti* knowledge;
one who studies this *Atharvaśiras* in the morning [destroys] the sin committed during the night.
It removes [evil]. One who studies in the evening removes the evil committed during the day.
By practicing this both in the evening and in the morning, one who was sinful becomes sinless.
One should study at midday while facing the sun.

One is liberated from the five great sins and the minor sins; one obtains the merit of having studied all the Vedas and Purāṇas; and one attains union with the Supreme Lord Viṣṇu—thus ends the Upaniṣad. 12.

He states the fruit of this knowledge: "This," etc. What need is there for much? One attains union (*sāyujya*) with the Great Lord Viṣṇu. The word "Upaniṣad" is used here to signify the completion of the *Mahāvākya-upaniṣad*. || 12 ||
This brief commentary on the Mahāvākya Upaniṣad has been written by Upadeśabrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra.
The Mahāvākyavivṛti, however, consists of thirty-two verses in length.
Thus ends the commentary on the Mahāvākya Upaniṣad, constituting the ninety-second [treatise] in the commentary on the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads, the sacred scripture.
